assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, let many atoms be interrogated Doppler- and recoil-free at once, pushing fractional uncertainty to the 1e-18 level. This is the clearest case of better measurement opening new physics: redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy, tests of constant variation and dark-matter searches. The concept is simple, original and decisive.
assessment.attribution: Katori made the conceptual invention and first realization of the magic-wavelength lattice clock; Ye's group brought the strontium lattice clock to record accuracy and stability and carried out the key comparisons. Both are credited and no other name is needed. Hall and Haensch (2005) and Wineland (2012) already covered the comb and ion clocks, which does not conflict with this credit.
assessment.maturity: Many independent labs worldwide (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, NPL) confirm the performance, clocks are routinely compared, and the redefinition of the second is being prepared. Recognition is timely and the physics is stable.
uncertainties: Whether the prize may be seen as an engineering refinement of the earlier Hall and Wineland recognition for atomic clocks and combs.
I am relying on memory for details of priority between Katori's proposal and parallel ideas, which I have not verified independently.
Ye also appears in the ultracold-molecule candidate, so the credit may be spread across lists.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms gives inertial, gravitational and rotational sensors of extreme sensitivity, with applications ranging from measuring G and the fine-structure constant to testing the equivalence principle and gravitational-wave detection concepts. It is a natural continuation of laser cooling and fits what is limited by what we can measure and how accurately.
assessment.attribution: Bordé theorized the atom-interferometer gyroscope and Ramsey-Bordé geometry, Pritchard demonstrated atom interferometry with gratings and later with light-pulse schemes, and Kasevich with Chu made the laser-based light-pulse gravimeter and gyroscope. Chu is not in the credited list, so only the three supplied names can be used. Selecting three from this field is difficult.
assessment.maturity: Field-deployed gravimeters, long-baseline interferometers and precision constant measurements are robust and reproduced across many groups. Mature, though the biggest fundamental-physics payoffs are still ahead.
uncertainties: Missing Steven Chu from the credited names weakens the configuration since his light-pulse work was foundational.
Priority claims between Bordé, Pritchard, Chu and Kasevich are disputed and I have not independently verified them.
Part of the credit may be considered already covered by the 1997 laser-cooling prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal showed how to implement quantum gates with laser-cooled trapped ions, creating the first concrete architecture for quantum computation. Experimental realization by Blatt and others turned it into a platform with the highest gate fidelities and clean quantum control of single particles. Foundational for quantum information science.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the 1995 proposal; Blatt's group realized the Cirac-Zoller gate and led teleportation and scalable experiments. Wineland and Haroche were recognized in 2012 for ion and cavity control, and some experimentalist credit (Monroe, Wineland group) is outside the supplied names. The three-name configuration is plausible and fair.
assessment.maturity: Over two decades of independent confirmation in Innsbruck, NIST, Maryland and industry-scale devices, and the interpretation is stable. Timely, though the quantum-computing prize landscape after the 2025 circuit prize is delicate.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 ion-trapping prize may weigh against novelty.
Whether the theory credit and experimental credit should be given together or one is premature relative to a larger quantum-computing prize.
Role of Cirac and Zoller in the optical-lattice and Rydberg candidates may lead to competing configurations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond opened room-temperature solid-state quantum sensing of magnetic fields, temperature and strain at nanoscale resolution, with a very broad reach into biology and materials. It relies on optical spin readout and microwave control, techniques familiar from my own field of coherent optics.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup's group first detected single NV centres optically (1997) and Jelezko, with Wrachtrup, demonstrated coherent spin control (2004). Lukin made major contributions to quantum registers and nanoscale magnetometry, and Awschalom, Hanson and others contributed. I would restrict the proposal to the first two, which has the cleanest priority, while acknowledging Lukin is a credible third.
assessment.maturity: Many groups confirm results, commercial sensors exist and applications are widespread. Quantum-sensing applications are still developing, but the underlying discovery is mature.
uncertainties: Whether a three-person prize should include Lukin for sensing and register work rather than only the first detection and control.
Large community and overlapping credit with spin-photon interface work in B027.
Practical impact in biology remains partially aspirational.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect introduced a new classification of electronic phases with protected edge and surface states and had a major conceptual influence across condensed matter. It is original and clean, although it lies outside my own specialism, so I weight it with deference to colleagues.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the theoretical prediction of the Z2 quantum spin Hall state; Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposed HgTe, which is not in the credited list, and Molenkamp's group realized it experimentally. The three supplied names offer a fair theory plus experiment configuration.
assessment.maturity: Extensive independent confirmation by ARPES and transport in many materials; the interpretation is stable. Following the 2016 topological-phases prize, the novelty is partly absorbed.
uncertainties: Missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang from the credited names complicates the fair attribution.
Whether it is timely given the 2016 prize for topological phase transitions.
I am an atomic physicist, so this assessment depends on general knowledge rather than detailed expertise.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realized Hubbard-model physics, the superfluid-Mott transition and quantum-gas microscopy, giving a controllable platform for many-body quantum simulation. This builds directly on laser cooling and Bose-Einstein condensation technology and has scientific depth.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realization; Greiner and Bloch carried out the Mott transition and then the quantum-gas microscope. Dalibard and Cirac are also credited, and Hansch and Greiner share roles. With a five-name list the selection is delicate and the three chosen are my best reading, not a settled division.
assessment.maturity: Strong independent confirmation in many groups and a mature subfield, but the headline simulation goals are still developing.
uncertainties: Five credited names suggest unresolved credit, and Greiner's role relative to Bloch and Dalibard is a judgement call.
Zoller overlap with trapped ions and Rydberg arrays.
Whether quantum simulation has produced a decisive new physical result yet.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution is a conceptually original application of quantum mechanics to secure communication, based on measurement disturbance and entanglement. It has had large impact on quantum information, with commercial and satellite links.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard proposed BB84 and Ekert proposed entanglement-based E91; the three names make a natural, widely cited configuration. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is outside the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Experimental QKD is well confirmed over fibre and satellite, though practical security and deployment are still evolving. The 2022 prize for entangled-photon experiments partly covered the foundations.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 Bell-test prize may reduce novelty.
Practical security loopholes and limited real-world adoption.
Wiesner's earlier contribution is not in the supplied credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold molecules, produced through buffer-gas cooling, direct laser cooling and association, extend atomic control to molecular degrees of freedom and enable precision tests such as the electron electric dipole moment as well as quantum chemistry and simulation. It is promising and close to my area of interest.
assessment.attribution: Doyle, DeMille and Ye contributed to cooling, trapping and precision measurements in different molecular routes; the supplied trio is plausible but different sub-discoveries (association versus direct cooling versus eEDM) make it a compound candidate with unclear primary credit. Ye overlaps with rank 1.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly developing; direct laser cooling and tweezer assembly are recent and the strongest scientific results are still being established. Probably somewhat early.
uncertainties: Compound discovery with several routes and possibly missing names such as Bohn, Jin, Ni and Ospelkaus.
Maturity is moderate and recognition may be premature.
Ye is also credited in the optical lattice clock candidate.
